samples.text:
The map shows the town of Hadley and two possible routes for a new bypass road. Overall, route 1 goes around the north of the town and route 2 goes around the south, and both of them start and finish at the A12.

Hadley town centre is in the middle of the map and the A12 go into it from the west and leave it to the east. There is housing in the north and in the south of the town centre. The River Hale runs from north to south on the west side of the town. There is a school in the north-west, trees in the north-east and farmland in the south-east.

Route 1 starts from the A12 in the west and goes north, near to the school. Then it cross the river and passes to the north of the housing. After that it goes through the north part of the woodland and comes down to the A12. Route 2 goes to south. It crosses the river too and passes the south of the housing, then it goes through the farmland before it join the A12.
samples.why: Overview present · both routes described in sequence with relevant features · formulaic linking (Then, After that) · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and preposition errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The map illustrates two proposed routes for a bypass around the town of Hadley. Overall, both routes would leave the A12 to the west of the town and rejoin it to the east, but Route 1 would pass to the north, near the school and through woodland, whereas Route 2 would run to the south, crossing farmland.

At present, the A12 enters Hadley from the west and continues through the town centre before leaving towards the east. The centre is surrounded by housing to the north and south, while the River Hale flows from north to south to the west of the town. A school is located in the north-west, with woodland in the north-east and farmland in the south-east.

Route 1 would curve northwards from the A12, passing close to the school, before crossing the river and running along the northern edge of the map, beyond the housing. It would then cut through the northern part of the woodland before turning south to meet the A12.

Route 2, by contrast, would head south-east, cross the river and pass well to the south of the housing. In the east, it would cut across the farmland before rejoining with the A12.
samples.why: Clear overview comparing the routes · each route traced logically · good use of contrast and sequencing · appropriate vocabulary (curve, cut through, rejoin) · mostly accurate with a minor slip.

samples.text:
The map shows the town of Hadley together with two alternative routes proposed for a bypass. Both routes would divert traffic from the A12 around the town, branching off to the west and rejoining it to the east; the key difference is that the northern option would affect the school and the woodland, while the southern option would cross farmland.

Currently, the A12 runs directly through Hadley town centre from west to east. The centre is flanked by housing to the north and south, and the River Hale flows southwards to the west of the town. The surrounding area contains a school in the north-west, woodland in the north-east and farmland in the south-east.

Route 1 would swing north from the A12, skirting the school closely on its western side, then cross the river and run parallel to the northern boundary of the map, well beyond the housing. It would subsequently cut through the northern fringe of the woodland before descending to meet the A12 east of the town.

Route 2 would follow a mirror-image course to the south. After crossing the river, it would pass some distance south of the housing and then bisect the farmland in the south-east before looping north to rejoin the A12.
samples.why: Sharp overview highlighting the key trade-off · both routes traced with precise reference to landmarks · sophisticated cohesion · accurate, wide vocabulary (skirting, fringe, mirror-image) · varied structures, error-free.
